passage:
The following text is adapted from Margaret Oliphant's 1866 novel Miss Marjoribanks. The text is an excerpt from a letter by Mrs. Irene Johansson to Mr. Antoine Elliott, in which Mrs. Johansson discusses an upcoming season at the seaside planned by her family.

Nothing would gratify us more than to extend our circle by including your dear Cecilia, who would be cared for and chaperoned with precisely the same attention as my own Margaret. Pray do not recoil at the suggestion; the time is surely come when she ought to know a little of society. When the young are kept too strictly within doors, their warm and untried fancies represent the world to them as some forbidden enchantment from which they have been unjustly excluded; but when they are introduced to it gradually, and at the proper season, they perceive it for what it truly is—a mingling, in equal measure, of comfort and trial, of expectation and regret.
prompt: Based on the text, Mrs. Johansson would most likely agree with which statement about Mr. Elliott?

choices.A: Although the manner in which he has educated Cecilia is in many respects admirable, he has erred in keeping her apart from the company of other young women.
choices.B: He has communicated to Cecilia his own romantic conception of the world, which has left her unprepared for the disappointments she must inevitably meet.
choices.C: Although his wish to guard Cecilia against unworthy acquaintances is laudable, his suspicious temperament has rendered him unjustly distrustful of her family.
choices.D: He is excessively cautious where Cecilia is concerned and would do well to permit her a wider range of experiences than she has so far enjoyed.

explanation: Choice D is the best answer. Mrs. Johansson writes to urge Mr. Elliott to allow his ward Cecilia to join her family at the seaside. Her words 'Pray do not recoil at the suggestion' indicate she anticipates Mr. Elliott will resist the proposal, and she goes on to argue that young people who are 'kept too strictly within doors' develop distorted, idealized views of the world, while those introduced to it 'gradually, and at the proper season' come to see it accurately. Together, these comments imply that Mrs. Johansson regards Mr. Elliott as too cautious in restricting Cecilia and believes Cecilia would benefit from broader experience than she has had thus far.
